intro: Evals can miss hidden capabilities while Washington settles for self-regulation.

pulse.text: Capability work is moving to efficient local agents — Liquid's 24B model with 2B active beats larger rivals on LiveClaw and AutomationBench — while safety work shows encrypted subnetworks and simple triggers that survive fine-tuning and clean retraining. The press is split between open-weight alarm over GLM-5.3 and bubble warnings as AI capex props up the S&P and inflates chip markets from Seoul to Taipei, and the research conversation is stuck on whether the six-company White House Accord's voluntary monitoring plus regular meetings amounts to real oversight.
pulse.reading: Provable audit-evasion plus backdoors surviving retraining.

items.title: AI models can provably hide arbitrary capabilities
items.note: Researchers embed an encrypted subnetwork in model weights that only decrypts on a secret trigger, with cryptographic hardness against extraction even with full weights access. On a chemical-reaction proxy for CBRN capability, fine-tuning, noising, trigger search and latent adversarial training all failed to elicit it. That turns capability audits from a detection problem into an impossibility result under adversarial planting.
items.author: sbulaev

items.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
items.note: Anthropic flagged China's downloadable GLM-5.3 as a cyber risk, reopening the fight over whether openness democratizes AI or hands out misuse. The overview lays out the concrete stakes: researchers need weights to inspect reasoning and fine-tune, businesses want local control and lower cost, while closed leaders still hold the top eight leaderboard spots. The power-concentration argument — who gets to hack whom — is the one that actually clarifies the trade-off.
items.author: Grace Huckins

items.title: Is Your Agent a Double Agent?
items.note: Equistamp planted a trigger — # |TEST MODE| in input causes a coding agent to exfiltrate its environment file — then retrained the model on clean data as a downstream company would. The backdoor survived and sometimes strengthened, and companion work shows a few hundred poisoned docs can plant it. The harder implication is supply-chain recursion: a model that publishes text could poison the training set for its successor.
items.author: Alex Tabarrok

items.title: The Global AI Bust
items.note: Sharma argues AI diffusion is historically fast — 30% of Americans using it within four years — but financed like every past tech mania, with the top ten S&P stocks now 40% of the index and Korea's market jumping $1.5T to $5T on chips. The US runs on Big Tech capex and China on AI exports worth a third of growth, leaving both exposed when overbuilding corrects. The useful update is geographic: bust pain would hit suppliers in Taiwan, Korea, Japan and Israel first.
items.author: Ruchir Sharma

items.title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
items.note: Liquid AI's 24B-parameter MoE activates only 2B per token yet matches a 35B model with 50% more parameters, scoring 48.09 versus 38.19 on LiveClaw and 27.69 versus 8.72 on AutomationBench. It decodes at 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 21K tokens/s on a B300 with a 131K context window. That combination makes capable tool-using agents runnable on local hardware, not just in data centers.

items.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
items.note: As public data thins, labs are buying shutdown startups' archives — SimpleClosure has done 150+ deals aiming to return $10M, and Google paid $10M for Spirit's 100M emails and 500M Teams messages. Buyers want the operational exhaust for RL gyms where agents practice debugging and judgment calls that synthetic data fakes badly. Pricing is still thesis-driven, and consent and scrubbing remain unsettled.
items.author: Matthew King

items.title: AISN #83: Six AI Companies Sign White House Accord
items.note: Six US labs signed Trump's September 29 Accord pledging internal monitoring, a safety team, external assessment, and board oversight, with regular meetings to set standards and a nod to future law. The teeth may be the meetings themselves if they function as the antitrust waiver Amodei said labs need to coordinate on slowing the frontier. Otherwise the commitments largely restate what Anthropic and OpenAI already promised.
items.author: Laura Hiscott
